compiled_state.description:
Make a stale clone's push **refuse** instead of silently re-unioning ~1 GiB of stripped history.
This is the keystone that makes the reclaim safe, and it must be deployed everywhere before the
window. session_log **1cb6-d553-6565-49b4** (measured facts; do not re-derive).

## Why a guard is needed at all, and why in two places
After the strip, `.bridge_state` still only appears from 2026-06-11, so the first **1,029 commits are
byte-identical** and `merge-base HEAD origin/tickets` **SUCCEEDS** (measured). So `sync.py` does NOT
take its unrelated-histories branch — it reaches the ordinary **diverged** path (`sync.py:155-166`) and
unions normally. Quiescence does not close this.

And a guard in `sync.py` alone is **bypassed**: `push.py:216` and `:242` run an INDEPENDENT
`git merge <remote>/<branch>` on non-fast-forward rejection and then re-push (<=3 attempts), never
consulting `sync.py`. That is exactly the path a stale review-bot write takes. **[v2 CORRECTED — the earlier chain was
wrong; plan-review caught it]** Verified chain: `voter.py:719 emit_code_review_artifact(...)` -> `artifact_emit.py:56` ->
`rebar.create_ticket` -> `event_append.py:587` (`write_and_push`) -> `push.push_tickets_branch(...)` -> push
rejected non-FF -> `push.py` merge -> retry **succeeds**. The create path reaches `push_tickets_branch` directly through `event_append`, rather than through
`push_after_commit`. The complete current `push_after_commit` caller set is `claim.py:253`,
`delete.py:339,399`, `compact.py:647,766`, and `transition_close.py:762`; `push_after_commit` itself
then calls `push_tickets_branch` (`push.py:300`), so every one of those paths is covered by the same
push guard. The review-bot call is `voter.py:719 emit_code_review_artifact(...)`, implemented in
`artifact_emit.py:56`.

## Placement (precise — the wrong spot wedges every clone)
- Inside **`sync._union_merge`** (`sync.py:170`) — the sole shared callee of both `:152` and `:166`.
  **NOT** before the merge-base test at `sync.py:143`: that would also block the ff-adopt at `sync.py:158`,
  which is exactly how a merely-behind clone converges, wedging it permanently.
- Before both non-fast-forward `run_git(["merge", remote_ref])` calls inside `push_tickets_branch`.
- **NOT** at `lock.acquire()` (where `check_store_compat` already fires, `lock.py:546`): a blanket
  write block would also block the convergence operation, deadlocking the clone it rejects.

## Where the epoch lives
Add an `epoch` field to the **existing** `.store-compat.json` rather than a parallel marker.
Verified safe: `compat.py`'s `_analyze` validates only `format_version` and `required_capabilities`
via `.get()`, so **unknown keys are ignored** — an older binary neither crashes nor fails closed.
`compat.write_compat_record` deliberately never generates an epoch. Before the reclaim it leaves a
record epoch-absent; after the reclaim, if the checked-out record already carries a valid string epoch,
it preserves that value when stamping format/capabilities so initialization cannot erase the guard. A
non-string existing epoch is corrupt and is not preserved. `_record_path` reads only the **local
worktree**, so the guard needs its own `git show <remote_ref>:.store-compat.json` reader for the other
side. The only operation that creates a fresh epoch value is A6-1's re-add commit.
The A6-0a tests create the documented opaque string directly in temporary local and remote
records to exercise the matrix; no production generator is added by this story. A6-1's history
publication step writes the concrete value into the dynamically re-added `.store-compat.json`.

## Expand/contract — the FULL state matrix (plan-review E2/T1 remediation)
The earlier wording said only "`absent == absent` => compatible, `absent vs present` => abort",
which left two distinct absences conflated. Specify all of it. Two independent axes per side:
the **record** (`.store-compat.json`) may be absent or present, and within a present record the
**`epoch` field** may be absent or present.

| local | remote | behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| record absent | record absent | **compatible** (pre-feature store both sides; union proceeds) |
| record absent | record present, epoch absent | **compatible** |
| record present, epoch absent | record present, epoch absent | **compatible** (today's state) |
| epoch present | epoch present, equal | **compatible** |
| epoch present | epoch present, different | **ABORT** |
| epoch absent | epoch present | **ABORT** (local predates the rewrite) |
| epoch present | epoch absent | **ABORT** (remote predates local; refuse rather than guess) |
| either side | record present but **corrupt/unparseable** | **ABORT** (never silently treat as absent — mirrors `compat.py`'s existing corrupt-record rule) |
| remote ref unreadable (`git show` non-zero) | — | **ABORT**, distinguished in the message from "file absent" |

Note the last two rows: `git show <remote_ref>:.store-compat.json` exits non-zero **both** when the
file does not exist at that ref and when the ref itself cannot be read. These must be
distinguished in the log message, because the remedies differ (re-clone vs fix the remote).

**Epoch value format (plan-review E2 remediation — previously unspecified).** `epoch` is a JSON
**string**, opaque to comparison: compared for byte equality only, never ordered or parsed. Value =
the ISO-8601 UTC instant of the rewrite plus a short random suffix
(e.g. `"2026-08-14T09-31-07Z-4f2a"`), unique per rewrite and human-diagnosable in a log line. A
non-string `epoch` (number, object, null) is treated as **corrupt** -> ABORT, matching `compat.py`'s
existing type-strictness for `format_version`. Deliberately NOT a monotonic counter: ordering invites
"newer is probably fine" reasoning, and the only safe response to any mismatch is
refuse-and-re-clone.

The epoch **value** appears only in the reclaim's re-add commit. That way pre-window clones (both absent) merge
normally even holding unpushed work, while post-rewrite stale clones abort.

**The guard only binds binaries at or after this change** — older ones ignore the field. So the
reclaim window instead requires direct deployment evidence: an observed `reconcile-bridge.yml` run on a
descendant SHA, plus deployed review-bot and explicitly refreshed host-runtime epoch-refusal probes; A6-0b deployment receipt and persistent-clone convergence stay in the protocol. These per-writer observations under quiescence replace elapsed time.

## Control flow at each guard site (plan-review G6 remediation)
`logger.warning` describes the *message*, not the *control flow* — and at the `push.py` sites both
merges sit inside the `for attempt` retry loop, so warning-and-continuing would simply retry the
push. Specify both sites explicitly:

- **`sync._union_merge`**: log and **return without merging**. `reconverge` is best-effort by
  contract (its sole caller `reads.ensure_fresh` swallows everything), so a no-op return is the
  correct degradation — the clone simply stays un-converged instead of unioning.
- **`push.py` (before the merges at the non-FF retry)**: log and **abort the retry loop
  immediately** — specifically **`return` out of `push_tickets_branch`, not `break`** (plan-review G6
  remediation): after the loop, `push.py:280` emits only the generic `push failed after N retries` warning;
  `break` would emit that misleading message for an epoch abort, whereas `return` exits immediately
  with the push explicitly not-completed. Do not merge, do not
  re-push, do not consume further attempts. The push must
  surface as *not* completed while leaving both histories untouched. Because neither side is an
  ancestor after this non-fast-forward epoch mismatch, `fsck` must report `DIVERGED` as the
  operator-visible re-clone signal (not `PUSH_PENDING`, which is reserved for local-ahead state). Returning "success" would silently drop the local commits from the
  operator's view, and continuing the loop would burn attempts on a merge that must never happen.

## Message channel
`logger.warning`, **not** an exception: every caller of `sync.reconverge` is `reads.ensure_fresh`
(`reads.py:193` (with the nested bare exceptions at `:258` and `:260`)), which wraps it in a bare `except Exception: pass` inside a second bare
`except Exception: return`, so a raise is swallowed with **no output**. Visibility comes from the entrypoints' configured logging handlers, not Python's `lastResort`;
`rebar.__init__` attaches a `NullHandler`, so lastResort never fires. Known gap: `sync.push=async` spawns the push with
`stdout/stderr=DEVNULL` (`push.py:113-145`), so those clones get no message and rely on `fsck`'s
`DIVERGED` report.

## Out of scope, declared
`fsck_recover.py` cherry-picks dangling ticket commits with no epoch awareness — it creates new
commits rather than unioning a DAG, so blast radius is bounded. Also **not** covered: the CI bash
unions at `reconcile-bridge.yml:348` and `reconcile-bridge-canary.yml:240`, which are protected by
the window protocol (workflows disabled + no in-flight run asserted), not by this guard.

## Verification commands
- State-matrix and remote-read unit oracle: `pytest tests/unit/test_epoch_guard_matrix.py -v`.
- Real-clone union, fast-forward/ahead controls, and operator-stderr oracle:
  `pytest tests/integration/test_epoch_guard_reconciliation.py -v`.
- Push retry and `PUSH_PENDING` control flow:
  `pytest tests/unit/test_epoch_guard_matrix.py -k push_retry -v`.
- Existing store compatibility coverage: `pytest tests/unit/test_store_compat.py -v`.
- Repository gates: `make lint`, `make typecheck`, and `make test`.

## Rollback example
Suppose the authoritative rewritten branch carries epoch `E1` and a current clone also carries
`E1`. If an operator deliberately rolls the authoritative branch back to a pre-epoch commit, the
state becomes local-present `E1` versus remote-absent and the guard aborts; it never guesses that
the rollback makes union safe. Recovery is an explicit reset/re-clone from the chosen authoritative
branch. A supported code rollback that leaves the epoch-bearing store commit in place retains `E1`
through `write_compat_record`, so equal-epoch current binaries continue to converge.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] [code-verifiable] A clone on a **stale epoch** reaching `sync._union_merge`
      returns without merging and preserves both pre-operation refs exactly. Tier: **integration**
      in real temporary clones with divergent epochs. This is one RED case.
- [ ] [code-verifiable] A clone on a **stale epoch** reaching `push.py`'s non-FF retry
      returns without merging or re-pushing and preserves both pre-operation refs exactly. Tier:
      **integration** in real temporary clones with divergent epochs. This is the second RED case.
- [ ] [code-verifiable] Assert on the emitted **log record** (`caplog`), plus one **subprocess** run with
      `REBAR_SYNC_PUSH=always` proving the message reaches a real operator's stderr.
      `sync.push=async` is excluded by design.
- [ ] [code-verifiable] At the `push.py` site the retry loop **terminates immediately** on epoch mismatch: exactly
      **zero** merge invocations and **zero** further push attempts, and the push remains
      not-completed. Tier: **unit** with a counting shim on the git
      calls — the guard is a pure predicate plus a control-flow decision, so no real remote is needed;
      the earlier "integration" label contradicted its own unit proving command (plan-review COH).
      Proving command: `pytest tests/unit/test_epoch_guard_matrix.py -k push_retry -v`.
- [ ] [code-verifiable] After a guard-aborted non-fast-forward push, `fsck` reports
      `DIVERGED` and does not report `PUSH_PENDING`; local and remote tips remain byte-for-byte
      unchanged. Tier: **integration** with real temporary clones.
      Proving command: `pytest tests/integration/test_epoch_guard_reconciliation.py -k fsck -v`.
- [ ] [code-verifiable] At the `sync._union_merge` site the function **returns without merging** and the clone is left
      un-converged (not corrupted). Tier: **integration**.
- [ ] [code-verifiable] A merely-**behind** clone (matching epochs) still converges via ff-adopt, and a
      **strictly-ahead** clone still returns early — neither is blocked. Tier: **integration**. This
      is the negative control that catches the wedge-everything misplacement.
- [ ] [code-verifiable] **Every row of the state matrix** above is asserted, including the two distinct absences
      (record-absent vs record-present-epoch-absent) and the corrupt-record row. Tier: **unit**,
      table-driven over the matrix — one case per row, so a missing row fails the suite.
      Proving command: `pytest tests/unit/test_epoch_guard_matrix.py -v`.
- [ ] [code-verifiable] `git show` failing because the **ref** is unreadable produces a different message than the file
      being **absent** at a readable ref. Tier: **unit** with two fixtures.
      Proving command: `pytest tests/unit/test_epoch_guard_matrix.py -k remote_read -v`.
- [ ] [code-verifiable] An older binary reading a record that carries `epoch` does not error and does not fail closed.
      Tier: **unit** against `compat._analyze`.
- [ ] [code-verifiable] `write_compat_record` preserves an existing valid string epoch, leaves a pre-epoch record absent,
      and never generates a new epoch value. Tier: **unit** covering all three cases.
- [ ] [code-verifiable] The remote side is read via `git show <remote_ref>:.store-compat.json`, not the local worktree.
      Tier: **unit** with a fixture where local and remote records differ.

`src/rebar/_store/compat.py`, `src/rebar/_store/sync.py`, `src/rebar/_store/push.py`, tests
